card.summary_ko: 671년 당의 행군총관 설인귀가 신라를 질책하는 편지를 보내자 문무왕이 이에 답한 글로, 당 태종의 약속, 백제·고구려 정벌에서 신라가 한 일, 당의 배신에 대한 억울함을 조목조목 밝힙니다. 《삼국사기》 문무왕 11년 조에 실려 있습니다.
card.summary_en: In 671 the Tang commander Xue Rengui sent a letter reproaching Silla, and King Munmu answered it point by point: Taizong's promises, what Silla did in the campaigns against Baekje and Goguryeo, and its grievance at Tang betrayal. Recorded in the Samguk sagi under Munmu's eleventh year.
card.edition_ko: 중국어 위키문헌 「三國史記/卷07」(개정 2150497, 2022-06-11)에서 문무왕 11년 조의 설인귀 편지와 문무왕 답서를 발췌. 원저작 퍼블릭 도메인, 전사 CC BY-SA 4.0
card.edition_en: Chinese Wikisource 「三國史記/卷07」 (revision 2150497, 2022-06-11), excerpt: Munmu's eleventh-year entry with Xue Rengui's letter and the king's reply; original in the public domain, transcription CC BY-SA 4.0

notes.ko:
**저자** 이 글은 문무왕(재위 661–681, 이름 김법민)의 이름으로 신라 조정이 당나라 장수에게 보낸 외교 문서이며, 현재 형태로는 고려 문신 김부식(1075–1151)이 1145년에 편찬한 《삼국사기》에 실려 전합니다. 답서는 실무를 맡은 문장가가 지었을 것이며, 강수(强首)의 글로 보는 견해가 있으나 확실하지 않습니다. 김부식은 경주 김씨 출신의 고려 관료로 1135–36년 묘청의 서경 반란을 진압한 인물이며, 유교적 합리주의와 현실적 질서를 중시한 보수적 문신으로 평가됩니다. 후대의 신채호 등은 《삼국사기》를 사대주의적이라 비판했고, 이에 맞서 유교 사관의 합리적 서술이라는 옹호도 있어 평가가 갈립니다. 이 답서는 신라 왕실의 공식 입장이므로, 신라가 자신을 피해자로 내세우는 논리임을 염두에 두어야 합니다.

**시대적 맥락** 신라는 당과 연합해 660년 백제, 668년 고구려를 멸망시켰으나, 당은 웅진·계림·안동 등에 도독부·도호부를 두어 신라까지 지배하려 했습니다. 신라는 고구려 유민(안승)을 받아들이고 옛 백제 땅을 차지하며 맞섰고, 670년부터 나당전쟁이 벌어졌습니다. 671년 당의 설인귀가 편지로 신라를 책망하자 문무왕이 이 글로 답했습니다. 이후 신라는 675년 매소성, 676년 기벌포 전투 등을 거쳐 당군을 한반도에서 몰아냈다고 알려져 있습니다.

**배경** 《삼국사기》 신라본기 문무왕 11년(671) 조입니다. 이 판은 중국어 위키문헌의 전사본이며 첫 단락에는 빈칸(■)이 있습니다. 같은 권의 이후 연도 기사는 뺐습니다.

**의의** 고구려·백제 평정 과정에서 신라가 겪은 부담과 당의 약속 번복을 신라 쪽에서 가장 길게 서술한 자료로, 삼국 통일 과정과 나당 관계를 이해하는 기본 사료입니다.

**형식과 주제** 변려문의 성격이 강한 서한이며 고사와 대구가 많습니다. 설인귀의 편지는 신라의 배신을 꾸짖고, 문무왕의 답서는 연대순으로 기여를 열거해 반박합니다. 주제는 약속과 신의, 동맹과 배신, 소국의 자기 변호입니다.

**읽기 도움**
- 摠管(총관): 당의 군사 지휘관 직함. 都護(도호)·都督(도독): 당이 설치한 지배 관직.
- 平章(평장): 함께 상의하여 결정함.
- 歃血(삽혈): 맹세 때 짐승 피를 입술에 바름.
- 噬臍(서제): 배꼽을 물려 해도 닿지 않는다는 뜻으로 뒤늦은 후회.
- 雍齒(옹치)·丁公(정공): 한 고조 때 인물 비유. 옹치는 미운 사람이었는데 상을 받았고, 정공은 유방을 놓아주었다가 주살되었습니다.
- 乾封·龍朔·麟德·總章·咸亨: 당 고종의 연호.
- 某(모): 글쓴이가 자신의 이름을 가리는 표기, 곧 '나'.
- 平壤已南百濟土地는 '평양 이남과 백제의 땅'으로도, 다르게도 읽혀 해석이 나뉩니다.
notes.en:
**About the author** This is a diplomatic letter sent in the name of King Munmu of Silla (r. 661–681, personal name Kim Beop-min) to a Tang general, and in its present form it survives in the Samguk sagi, compiled in 1145 by the Goryeo official Kim Bu-sik (1075–1151). The reply would have been drafted by a skilled prose writer of the court; some attribute it to Gang Su, but this is not certain. Kim Bu-sik was a Gyeongju Kim and a Goryeo court official who suppressed Myocheong's Seogyeong rebellion in 1135–36; he is generally seen as a conservative Confucian official who valued rational, orderly government. Later critics such as Sin Chae-ho attacked the Samguk sagi as deferential to China (*sadae*), while others defend it as sober Confucian historiography, so assessments differ. As the reply states the official position of the Silla court, one should bear in mind that it argues Silla's case as a victim.

**Historical context** Silla allied with Tang to destroy Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668, but Tang set up protectorates and commanderies at Ungjin, Gyerim and Andong and sought to control Silla itself. Silla resisted by taking in Goguryeo refugees (Ansung) and occupying old Baekje land, and the Silla–Tang War began in 670. In 671 Xue Rengui reproached Silla by letter, and Munmu answered with this text. Silla is known to have driven Tang forces from the peninsula through battles such as Maesoseong in 675 and Gibeolpo in 676.

**Background** This is the Samguk sagi, Silla Annals, Munmu's eleventh year (671). The edition is the Chinese Wikisource transcription, with blanks (■) in the first paragraph. The entries for later years in the same volume are omitted.

**Significance** It is the longest account from the Silla side of the burdens Silla bore in the destruction of Goguryeo and Baekje and of Tang's reversal of its promises, and a basic source for the unification wars and Silla–Tang relations.

**Form and themes** An epistle in a strongly parallel-prose style, full of allusions and antitheses. Xue Rengui's letter scolds Silla for betrayal, while Munmu's reply answers by listing Silla's contributions in order of time. The themes are promises and good faith, alliance and betrayal, and a small state's self-defence.

**Reading help**
- 摠管 (chonggwan): a Tang military commander's title; 都護 (doho), 都督 (doduk): Tang governing posts.
- 平章 (pyeongjang): to deliberate and decide together.
- 歃血 (sap-hyeol): smearing animal blood on the lips in an oath.
- 噬臍 (seoje): "biting one's navel," i.e. regret that comes too late.
- 雍齒 (Yongchi), 丁公 (Jeonggong): figures from the Han founding. Yongchi was disliked yet rewarded; Ding Gong let Liu Bang go and was executed.
- 乾封, 龍朔, 麟德, 總章, 咸亨: reign-period names of Emperor Gaozong of Tang.
- 某 (mo): the writer's own name withheld, i.e. "I."
- 平壤已南百濟土地 can be read as "the lands south of Pyongyang and the lands of Baekje" or otherwise, and interpretations differ.

paragraphs.orig: 十一年，春正月，拜伊飡禮元爲中侍。發兵侵百濟，戰於熊津南。幢主夫果死之。靺鞨兵來圍舌口城，不克將退，出兵撃之，斬殺三百餘人。王聞唐兵欲來捄百濟，遣大阿飡眞功、阿飡■■、■■兵守甕浦。白魚躍入■■■■■■■■■■一寸。夏四月，震興輪寺南門。六月，遣將軍竹旨等，領兵踐百濟加林城禾，遂與唐兵戰於石城，斬首五千三百級，獲百濟將軍二人、唐果毅六人。秋七月二十六日，大唐摠管薛仁貴使琳潤法師寄書曰：
paragraphs.en: In the eleventh year, spring, first month, Ichan Yewon was appointed Jungsi. Troops were sent to invade Baekje and fought south of Ungjin; the banner commander Bubu died in it. Malgal troops came and besieged Seolgu Fortress; failing, as they were about to retreat, our troops sallied out and struck them, killing more than three hundred. The king, hearing that Tang troops were about to come to relieve Baekje, sent Daeachan Jingong, Achan [two characters missing] and [two characters missing] troops to guard Ongpo. A white fish leapt in [text missing] an inch. In summer, fourth month, thunder struck the south gate of Heungnyun Temple. In the sixth month, he sent the general Jukji and others to lead troops to trample the grain in Garim Fortress of Baekje, and then fought Tang troops at Seokseong, taking five thousand three hundred heads and capturing two Baekje generals and six Tang colonels. In autumn, seventh month, twenty-sixth day, the great Tang commander Xue Rengui sent the Dharma master Rimyun to deliver a letter, which said:

paragraphs.orig: 「行軍摠管薛仁貴致書新羅王。淸風萬里，大海三千，天命有期，行遵此境。奉承機心稍動，窮武邊城，去由也之片言，失侯生之一諾。兄爲逆首，弟作忠臣，遠分花蕚之陰，空照相思之月。興言彼此，良增歎詠。先王開府，謀猷一國，展轉百城，西畏百濟之侵，北警高麗之寇。地方千里，數處爭鋒，蠶女不及桑時，耘人失其疇序。年將耳順，楡景日侵，不懼船海之危，遠渉陽侯之險，瀝心華境，頓䫙天門，具陳孤弱，明論侵擾，情之所露，聽不勝悲。太宗文皇帝，氣雄天下，神王宇宙，若盤古之九變，同巨靈之一掌，扶傾救弱，日不暇給。哀納先君，矜收所請，輕車駿馬，美衣上藥，一日之内，頻遇殊私。亦既承恩，對揚軍事，契同魚水，明於金石。鳳鑰千重，鶴關萬戸，留連酒德，讌笑金除，叅論兵馬。分期聲援，一朝大擧，水陸交鋒。于時，塞草分花，楡星上莢。駐蹕之戰，文帝親行，吊人恤隱，義之深也。既而，山海異形，日月廻薄，聖人下武，王亦承家。巖葛因依，聲塵共擧，洗兵刷馬，咸遵先志。數十年外，中國疲勞，帑藏時開，飛蒭日給。以蒼島之地，起黄圖之兵，貴於有益，貪於無用。豈不知止，恐失先君之信也。今強寇已淸，讎人喪國，士馬玉帛，王亦有之。當應心膂不移，中外相輔，銷鏑而化，虚室爲情，自然貽厥孫謀，以燕翼子。良史之讚，豈不休哉？今王去安然之基，厭守常之策，遠乖天命，近棄父言，侮暴天時，侵欺鄰好，一隅之地，僻左之陬，率戸徴兵，連年擧斧，孀姫輓粟，稚子屯田。守無所支，進不能拒。以得裨喪，以存補亡，大小不侔，逆順乖敍，亦由持彈而往，暗於枯井之危，捕蟬而前，不知黄雀之難，此王之不知量也。先王在日，早蒙天睠，審懷險詖之心，假以披誠之禮，從己私欲，貪天至功，苟希前惠，圖爲後逆，此先君之不長者也。必其誓河若帶，義分如霜，違君之命不忠，背父之心非孝，一身二名，何以自寧？王之父子，一朝振立，此並天情遠及，威力相持，方州連郡，遂爲盤錯。從此，遽蒙冊命，拜以稱臣。坐治經書，備詳詩禮，聞義不從，見善而輕，聽縱橫之説，煩耳目之神，忽高門之基，延鬼瞰之責。先君盛業，奉而異圖，内潰疑臣，外招強陣，豈爲智也？又高麗安勝，年尚幼冲，遺壑殘郛，生人減半，自懷去就之疑，匪堪襟帶之重。仁貴樓船，竟翼風帆，連旗巡於北岸，矜其舊日傷弓之羽，未忍加兵，恃爲外援，斯何謬也！皇帝德澤無涯，仁風遠洎，愛同日景，炤若春華。遠聞消息，悄然不信，爰命下臣，來觀由委。而王不能行人相問，牛酒犒師，遂便隱甲雀陂，藏兵江口，蚑行林薄，喘息萊丘。潛生自㭀之鋒，而無相持之氣。大軍未出，游兵具行，望海浮江，魚驚鳥竄。以此形況，人事可求，沉迷猖惑，幸而知止。夫擧大事者，不貪小利，杖高節者，寄以英奇。必其鸞鳳不馴，豺狼有顧，高將軍之漢騎，李謹行之蕃兵，呉、楚棹歌，幽并惡少，四面雲合，方舟而下，依險築戍，闢地耕田，此王之膏肓也。王若勞者歌，事屈而頓申，具論所由，明陳彼此。仁貴夙陪大駕，親承委寄，録狀聞奏，事必昭蘇，何苦怱怱，自相縈擾。嗚呼，昔爲忠義，今乃逆臣，恨始吉而終凶，怨本同而末異。風高氣切，葉落年悲，憑山遠望，有傷懷抱。王以機䎸淸明，風神爽秀，歸以流謙之義，存於順迪之心，血食依時，茅苴不易，占休納祐，王之策也。嚴鋒之間，行人來往，今遣王所部僧琳潤書，佇布一二。」
paragraphs.en: "Xue Rengui, Commander of the Marching Army, sends this letter to the King of Silla. A clear wind of ten thousand li, a great sea of three thousand: Heaven's decree has its term, and I have come to this land. Having received our favour, your scheming heart began to stir, and you pushed your arms against the border cities, discarding the single word that Zilu would have needed and losing the one promise of Master Hou. The elder brother is a rebel chief, the younger brother a loyal subject; far apart in the shade of calyx and blossom, in vain does the moon of longing shine. Speaking of both of you, I truly add to my sighs and chants. Your late king set up his government and planned for one country, moving through a hundred cities; in the west he feared Baekje's incursions, in the north he was on guard against Goguryeo's raids. His land was a thousand li square, with contests of arms at several places; silkworm girls missed the mulberry season, farmers lost the order of their fields. Nearing the age of sixty, with the elm-light of sunset encroaching day by day, he did not fear the danger of crossing the sea by ship but travelled far across the perils of Yanghou's waves, poured out his heart in the Chinese realm and bowed his head at the heavenly gate, setting forth his isolation and weakness and clearly arguing the invasions; the feeling he revealed was unbearable to hear for its sadness. Emperor Taizong Wen, whose spirit towered over the world, a god-king of the universe, like Pangu's nine transformations, like the single palm of Juling, supported the fallen and rescued the weak, with not a day of leisure. He took pity on your late lord and received him, graciously accepting his requests: light carriages and swift horses, fine clothes and the best medicine, so that within a single day he repeatedly received special favour. Having received this grace, your lord answered in military affairs; the pact was like fish and water, clearer than metal and stone. Phoenix locks in a thousand layers, crane gates in ten thousand doors; they lingered in the virtue of wine, feasted and laughed on the golden steps, and joined in discussing troops and horses. They set a date for mutual support, and one morning the great campaign was launched, with land and sea forces in battle. At that time the frontier grass divided into flowers and the elm star put forth pods. In the battle of Zhubi, Emperor Wen went in person; to console the people and pity their suffering, the righteousness was deep. After that, mountains and sea changed form and sun and moon wheeled; the sage ruler followed in his footsteps, and the king too inherited the house. The cliff creepers clung and relied; voice and dust rose together; washing weapons and brushing horses, all followed the earlier will. For several decades China has been wearied, the treasury is opened from time to time, and fodder is supplied day by day. Raising troops of the yellow chart for the land of the blue island, valuing benefit and coveting what is useless, how could we not know when to stop? We feared to lose the trust of your late lord. Now the strong enemy has been cleared, the foe has lost his country, and soldiers, horses, jade and silk, the king has these as well. You should keep heart and spine steadfast, support each other within and without, melt the arrowheads and so transform them, make the empty chamber the ground of your feeling, and naturally leave plans to your descendants and shelter your sons under your wings. The praise of the good historian, would it not be splendid? Now the king leaves the foundation of peace and tires of the policy of keeping to the norm; far off he defies the Mandate of Heaven, near at hand he casts aside his father's words; he insults and tyrannizes the seasons of Heaven and invades and cheats a neighbour's good relations. In a corner of land, a remote nook on the left, you conscript soldiers household by household and raise axes year after year; widows haul grain, young children farm the garrison fields. Defence has nothing to rely on, advance cannot resist. You use gain to make up for loss and survival to supplement destruction; large and small are unequal, the contrary and the obedient are out of order. It is like going with a bullet-bow while blind to the danger of a dry well, or going forward to catch a cicada without knowing the hazard of the yellow sparrow behind; this is the king's failure to know his measure. When the late king was alive, he early received Heaven's regard, yet he harboured a perilous and crooked heart and borrowed the form of baring his sincerity, indulging his own private desires and coveting the highest merit of Heaven, seeking only the previous favour while plotting later rebellion; this was the late lord's lack of excellence. If it was truly the case that he swore 'though the Yellow River become a belt' and shared a righteousness firm as frost, then to defy your lord's command is disloyal and to go against your father's heart is unfilial; with one body and two names, how can you be at ease? You, father and son, were raised up in one morning; this was owing to Heaven's feeling reaching far and to the support of might; the provinces and commanderies were linked and then became tangled. From this you suddenly received investiture, were appointed and called yourselves subjects. Sitting, you studied the classics and books, fully versed in the Odes and Rites, yet hearing righteousness you did not follow it, seeing the good you took it lightly, listened to the talk of alliances and vertical-horizontal strategy and wearied the spirit of ear and eye, neglected the foundation of a high house and drew on the censure of ghostly glances. The great work of the late lord you accepted but plotted otherwise; within, you shattered the trust of ministers; without, you invited strong armies; is that wisdom? Moreover, Ansung of Goguryeo is still young; abandoned ravines and shattered outer walls, a population halved, he himself harbours doubts about going or staying and is not fit to bear the weight of being a bulwark. Rengui's tower ships, with sails like wings, linked banners patrolling the northern bank, pity his old-time bow-wounded wings and cannot bear to attack him; and you rely on him as external aid; what a mistake! The Emperor's grace has no bound, his benevolent wind reaches far, his love is like the sun's light and his brilliance like spring flowers. Hearing the news from afar, he was uneasy and did not believe it, and so he commissioned his humble servant to come and see the reasons. But you were not able to send an envoy to ask, nor to feast the army with ox and wine; instead you hid armour at Jakpa and concealed troops at the river mouth, creeping like crawling creatures in the thickets and gasping on the hills. Secretly you grew a blade to destroy yourself, yet had not the vigour to stand against us. The main army has not set out but roving troops have already gone; looking over the sea and floating on the rivers, fish were startled and birds scattered. By this state of affairs, human affairs can be sought; you are deeply deluded and reckless, and by luck know when to stop. One who undertakes great things does not covet small gain; one who relies on lofty integrity entrusts his charge to the talented. If the simurgh and phoenix are not tamed and the jackals and wolves look back, then General Gao's Han cavalry, Li Jinxing's barbarian troops, the oar songs of Wu and Chu, the evil youths of You and Bing will gather from four sides like clouds, come down in paired boats, build garrisons on strongholds, open land and farm fields; this will be the king's incurable disease. If the king, like the labourer who sings out his hardship, will bend in his case and then stretch, state in full the reasons and clearly set forth this and that, then Rengui, who has long attended the great carriage and personally received the commission, will record the circumstances and report them, and the matter will surely be cleared. Why trouble yourselves in such haste, entangling and disturbing one another? Alas! Once loyal and righteous, now a rebellious subject; I regret that it began in good fortune and ended in ill, I resent that the origins were the same and the ends different. The wind is high and the air cutting, leaves fall and the year is sad; leaning on the mountains to gaze afar, I am hurt in my heart. As the king has a bright and clear intellect and a fine and elegant bearing, return to the principle of humility and keep a mind that follows the right way; let the blood-sacrifices be offered in season and the offerings not be changed, and seek blessings and receive divine help; this is the king's course. Among sharp blades, envoys come and go; now I send this letter by the king's own subordinate, the monk Rimyun, and wait to set out one or two things."
The Great King replied by letter, saying:

paragraphs.orig: 「先王貞觀二十二年，入朝，面奉太宗文皇帝恩勅。『朕今伐高麗，非有他故，憐伱新羅，攝乎兩國，毎被侵陵，靡有寧歳。山川土地，非我所貪，玉帛子女，是我所有。我平定兩國，平壤已南百濟土地、並乞伱新羅，永爲安逸。』垂以計會，賜以軍期。新羅百姓，具聞恩勅，人人畜力，家家待用。大事未終，文帝先崩，今帝踐祚，復繼前恩，頻蒙慈造，有踰往日。兄弟及兒，懷金拖紫，榮寵之極，夐古未有。粉身碎骨，望盡驅馳之用，肝腦塗原，仰報萬分之一。至顯慶五年，聖上感先志之未終，成曩日之遺緖，泛舟命將，大發船兵。先王年衰力弱，不堪行軍，追感前恩，勉強至於界首，遣某領兵，應接大軍。東西唱和，水陸倶進，船兵纔入江口，陸軍已破大賊。兩軍倶到王都，共平一國。平定已後，先王遂共蘇大摠管平章，留漢兵一萬，新羅亦遣弟仁泰，領兵七千，同鎭熊津。大軍廻後，賊臣福信，起於江西，取集餘燼，圍逼府城，先破外柵，摠奪軍資，復攻府城，幾將陷沒。又於府城側近四處，作城圍守，於此，府城不得出入。某領兵往赴解圍，四面賊城，並皆打破，先救其危，復運粮食，遂使一萬漢兵，免虎吻之危難，留鎭餓軍，無易子而相食。至六年，福信徒黨漸多，侵取江東之地，熊津漢兵一千，往打賊徒，被賊摧破，一人不歸。自敗已來，熊津請兵，日夕相繼。新羅多有疫病，不可徴發兵馬，苦請難違，遂發兵衆，往圍周留城。賊知兵小，遂即來打，大損兵馬，失利而歸。南方諸城，一時摠叛，並屬福信，福信乘勝，復圍府城。因即熊津道斷，絶於鹽豉，即募健兒，偸道送鹽，救其乏困。至六月，先王薨，送葬纔訖，喪服未除，不能應赴，勅旨發兵北歸。含資道摠管劉德敏等至，奉勅遣新羅供運平壤軍粮。此時，熊津使人來，具陳府城孤危。劉摠管與某平章自云：『若先送平壤軍粮，即恐熊津道斷，熊津若其道斷，留鎭漢兵，即入賊手。』劉摠管遂共某相隨，先打甕山城。既拔甕山，仍於熊津造城，開通熊津道路。至十二月，熊津粮盡。先運熊津，恐違勅旨，若送平壤，即恐熊津絶粮。所以差遣老弱，運送熊津，強健精兵，擬向平壤。熊津送粮，路上逢雪，人馬死盡，百不一歸。至龍朔二年正月，劉摠管 共 新羅兩河道摠管金庾信 等，同送平壤軍粮。當時陰雨連月，風雪極寒，人馬凍死，所將兵粮，不能勝致。平壤大軍，又欲歸還。新羅兵馬，粮盡亦廻。兵士饑寒，手足凍瘃，路上死者，不可勝數。行至瓠瀘河，高麗兵馬，尋後來趂，岸上列陣。新羅兵士，疲乏日久，恐賊遠趂，賊未渡河，先渡交刃，前鋒暫交，賊徒瓦解，遂收兵歸來。此兵到家，未經一月，熊津府城，頻索種子，前後所送，數萬餘斛。南運熊津，北供平壤，蕞小新羅，分供兩所，人力疲極，牛馬死盡，田作失時，年穀不熟，所貯倉粮，漕運並盡，新羅百姓，草根猶自不足，熊津漢兵，粮食有餘。又留鎭漢兵，離家日久，衣裳破壞，身無全褐。新羅勸課百姓，送給時服。都護劉仁願，遠鎭孤城，四面皆賊，恒被百濟侵圍，常蒙新羅解救。一萬漢兵，四年衣食新羅，仁願已下，兵士已上，皮骨雖生漢地，血肉倶是新羅。國家恩澤，雖復無涯，新羅效忠，亦足矜憫。至龍朔三年，摠管孫仁師領兵來救府城，新羅兵馬，亦發同征，行至周留城下。此時，倭國船兵，來助百濟，倭船千艘，停在白沙，百濟精騎，岸上守船。新羅驍騎，爲漢前鋒，先破岸陣，周留失膽，遂即降下。南方已定，廻軍北伐，任存一城，執迷不降。兩軍併力，共打一城，固守拒捍，不能打得。新羅即欲廻還，杜大夫云：『準勅，既平已後，共相盟會，任存一城，雖未降下，即可共相盟誓。』新羅以爲。準勅，『旣平。』已後，共相盟會，任存未降，不可以爲『旣平。』又且百濟，姦詐百端，反覆不恒，今雖共相盟會，於後恐有噬臍之患，奏請停盟。至麟德元年，復降嚴勅，責不盟誓，即遣人於熊嶺，築壇共相盟會。仍於盟處，遂爲兩界。盟會之事，雖非所願，不敢違勅。又於就利山築壇，對勅使劉仁願，歃血相盟，山河爲誓，畫界立封，永爲疆界，百姓居住，各營産業。至乾封二年，聞大摠管英國公征遼，某往漢城州，遣兵集於界首。新羅兵馬，不可獨入，先遣細作三度，船相次發遣，覘候大軍。細作廻來，並云：『大軍未到平壤。』且打高麗七重城，開通道路，佇待大軍來至。其城垂垂欲破，英公使人江深來云。『奉大摠管處分，新羅兵馬不須打城，早赴平壤，即給兵粮。』遣令赴會，行至水谷城，聞大軍已廻，新羅兵馬，遂即抽來。至乾封三年，遣大監金寶嘉入海，取英公進止。奉處分，新羅兵馬，赴集平壤。至五月，劉右相來，發新羅兵馬，同赴平壤。某亦往漢城州，檢校兵馬。此時，蕃、漢諸軍，摠集虵水，男建出兵，欲決一戰。新羅兵馬，獨爲前鋒，先破大陣，平壤城中，挫鋒縮氣。於後，英公更取新羅驍騎五百人，先入城門，遂破平壤，克成大功。於此新羅兵士並云：『自征伐已經九年，人力殫盡，終始平兩國，累代長望，今日乃成，必當國蒙盡忠之恩，人受効力之賞。』英公漏云：『新羅前失軍期，亦須計定。』新羅兵士得聞此語，更增怕懼。又立功軍將，並録入朝，已到京下，即云：『今新羅並無功。』夫軍將歸來，百姓更加怕懼。又卑列之城，本是新羅，高麗打得三十餘年，新羅還得此城，移配百姓，置官守捉，又取此城，還與高麗。且新羅自平百濟，迄定高麗，盡忠効力，不負國家，未知何罪，一朝遺棄。雖有如此寃枉，終無反叛之心。至總章元年，百濟於盟會處，移封易標，侵取田地，詃我奴婢，誘我百姓，隱藏内地，頻從索取，至竟不還。又通消息云：『國家修理船艘，外託征伐倭國，其實欲打新羅。』百姓聞之，驚懼不安。又將百濟婦女，嫁與新羅漢城都督朴都儒，同謀合計，偸取新羅兵器，襲打一州之地，賴得事覺，即斬都儒，所謀不成。至咸亨元年六月，高麗謀叛，摠殺漢官。新羅即欲發兵，先報熊津云：『高麗既叛，不可不伐，彼此倶是帝臣，理須同討凶賊，發兵之事，須有平章，請遣官人來此，共相計會。』百濟司馬禰軍來此，遂共平章云：『發兵已後，即恐彼此相疑，宜令兩處官人，互相交質。』即遣金儒敦及府城百濟主簿首彌、長貴等，向府平論交質之事。百濟雖許交質，城中仍集兵馬，到彼城下，夜即來打。至七月，入朝使金欽純等至，將畫界地，案圖披檢百濟舊地，摠令割還。黄河未帶，太山未礪，三四年間，一與一奪，新羅百姓，皆失本望，並云：『新羅、百濟累代深讎，今見百濟形況，別當自立一國，百年已後，子孫必見呑滅。新羅既是國家之州，不可分爲兩國。願爲一家，長無後患。』去年九月，具録事狀，發使奏聞，被漂却來。更發遣使，亦不能達。於後，風寒浪急，未及聞奏。百濟構架奏云：『新羅反叛。』新羅前失貴臣之志，後被百濟之譖，進退見咎，未申忠欵。似是之讒，日經聖聽，不貳之忠，曾無一達。使人琳潤至辱書，仰承摠管，犯冒風波，遠來海外，理須發使郊迎，致其牛酒，遠居異城，未獲致禮，時闕迎接，請不爲怪。披讀摠管來書，專以新羅已爲叛逆，既非本心，惕然驚懼。數自功夫，恐被斯辱之譏，緘口受責，亦入不弔之數，今略陳寃枉，具録無叛。國家不降一介之使，垂問元由。即遣數萬之衆，傾覆巢穴，樓船滿於滄海，艫舳連於江口，數彼熊津，伐此新羅。嗚呼。兩國未定平，蒙指蹤之驅馳，野獸今盡，反見烹宰之侵逼。賊殘百濟，反蒙雍齒之賞，殉漢新羅，已見丁公之誅。大陽之曜，雖不廻光，葵藿本心，猶懷向日。摠管禀英雄之秀氣，抱將相之高材，七德兼備，九流渉獵，恭行天罰，濫加非罪。天兵未出，先問元由。縁此來書，敢陳不叛，請摠管審自商量，具狀申奏。林州大都督左衛大將軍開府儀同三司上柱國新羅王金法敏白。」
paragraphs.en: "In the twenty-second year of Zhenguan, the late king went to court and personally received a gracious edict from Emperor Taizong Wen: 'I am now attacking Goguryeo for no other reason than that I pity you, Silla, hemmed between two countries, always invaded and without a peaceful year. Mountains, rivers and lands are not what I covet; jade, silk, sons and daughters I already possess. When I have pacified the two countries, the lands south of Pyongyang and the lands of Baekje I will grant entirely to you, Silla, to be your peace and ease forever.' He laid down plans and set the date for the campaign. The people of Silla all heard this gracious edict; every person stored up strength and every household waited to be used. Before the great matter was finished, Emperor Wen died; the present emperor ascended the throne and continued the former favour, repeatedly granting his kind creation, exceeding what went before. Brothers and sons wore gold and trailed purple, the height of glory and favour, such as has not been since remote antiquity. We wished to grind our bodies and crush our bones in the service of your driving, to smear our livers and brains on the plains to repay a ten-thousandth part. In the fifth year of Xianqing, the Sage Ruler, moved that the former will was unfinished and to complete the remaining task of former days, launched ships and appointed generals and sent out his fleet in force. The late king, aged and weak, could not bear to take the field, but recalling the former favour he forced himself to the border and sent me at the head of troops to respond to the great army. East and west calling and answering, land and sea advancing together, the fleet had only just entered the river mouth when the land army had already broken the great enemy. The two armies arrived together at the royal capital and together pacified one country. After the pacification, the late king consulted with Great Commander Su, and ten thousand Han troops were left behind; Silla also sent his younger brother In-tae with seven thousand troops, and together they garrisoned Ungjin. After the main army withdrew, the rebel minister Bokshin rose west of the river, gathered the embers that remained, besieged and pressed the prefectural city, first broke the outer palisade and seized all the military supplies, and attacked the city again, so that it almost fell. Also at four places near the city they built fortresses to encircle it, so that the city could not be entered or left. I led troops to its relief; the rebel forts on all four sides I broke, first rescuing them from danger, and then again carried grain, so that ten thousand Han troops escaped the peril of the tiger's mouth, and the starving garrison did not have to exchange children to eat. In the sixth year Bokshin's band grew gradually and encroached on the land east of the river; a thousand Han troops from Ungjin went to attack the rebels and were crushed by them, and not one returned. Ever since that defeat, requests for troops from Ungjin came one after another day and evening. Silla had much epidemic disease and could not levy troops, but the pleas were bitter and hard to refuse, and so I sent out troops and they went to besiege Juryu Fortress. The rebels knew our force was small, came to attack, greatly damaged our troops and horses, and we returned without success. The fortresses of the south all at once rebelled and joined Bokshin; Bokshin, riding his victory, again besieged the prefectural city. Thereupon the Ungjin road was cut and salt and fermented beans ran out, so I at once recruited sturdy men to carry salt by secret roads and relieve their want. In the sixth month the late king died; the funeral had only just ended and the mourning clothes were not yet removed, so I could not respond to the summons, but an imperial edict ordered troops to go north. The commander of the Hamja Road, Liu Deming and others, arrived bearing an edict that ordered Silla to supply grain to the Pyongyang army. At this time envoys came from Ungjin and fully reported the isolation and danger of the prefectural city. Commander Liu consulted with me and said: 'If we first send grain to the Pyongyang army, I fear the Ungjin road will be cut, and if the Ungjin road is cut, the Han troops left to garrison it will fall into rebel hands.' Commander Liu then went with me and first attacked Ongsan Fortress. Once Ongsan was taken, we built a fortress at Ungjin and opened the road to Ungjin. In the twelfth month Ungjin's grain ran out. To send first to Ungjin we feared to disobey the edict; to send to Pyongyang we feared Ungjin would run out of grain. So we dispatched the old and weak to carry grain to Ungjin, while the strong and the elite troops were intended for Pyongyang. The grain sent to Ungjin met snow on the road, and men and horses died to the last, and not one in a hundred came back. In the first month of the second year of Longshuo, Commander Liu together with Kim Yu-sin, commander of Silla's two river roads, and others sent grain to the Pyongyang army. At that time cloudy rain continued for months, wind and snow were extremely cold, men and horses froze to death, and the troops could not bring the grain they carried. The great army at Pyongyang again wished to withdraw. Silla's troops, their grain exhausted, also turned back. The soldiers were hungry and cold, their hands and feet frostbitten, and those who died on the road could not be counted. On reaching the Horo River, the Goguryeo troops came after us and drew up in formation on the bank. Silla's soldiers had long been exhausted and feared the enemy would pursue far; before the enemy crossed the river, we crossed first to engage; when the vanguards had briefly clashed, the enemy collapsed like roof tiles, and we gathered our troops and returned. When these troops reached home, not a month had passed before the Ungjin prefectural city repeatedly asked for seed; what was sent in all came to more than tens of thousands of hu. South to Ungjin and north to Pyongyang, tiny Silla supplied two places separately; people's strength was exhausted, oxen and horses all died, fieldwork lost its season, the year's grain did not ripen, and the stored granary grain was all used up in transport; the people of Silla did not even have enough roots of grass, while the Han troops at Ungjin had surplus grain. The Han troops left in garrison, moreover, long away from home, had clothes in ruins and not a whole garment on their bodies. Silla urged the people to send them seasonal clothing. The Protector-General Liu Renyuan, garrisoning a lonely city far away with enemies on all four sides, was constantly besieged by Baekje and constantly rescued by Silla. For four years ten thousand Han troops were clothed and fed by Silla; from Renyuan down to the soldiers above [a certain rank], though their skin and bones were born in the land of Han, their flesh and blood were all Silla's. The imperial grace is, to be sure, boundless, but Silla's loyal service is also worthy of compassion. In the third year of Longshuo, Commander Sun Renshi led troops to relieve the prefectural city, and Silla's troops also set out to join the expedition and came to the foot of Juryu Fortress. At this time the Wa fleet came to help Baekje; a thousand Wa ships anchored at Baeksa, and Baekje's elite cavalry guarded the ships on the shore. Silla's brave cavalry, as the vanguard of the Han, first broke the formation on the bank; Juryu lost heart and at once surrendered. The south being settled, the army turned back to campaign north, but one fortress, Imjon, stubbornly clung to its delusion and would not surrender. The two armies joined strength to attack one fortress; it held firm and resisted, and could not be taken. Silla wished to turn back, but Grand Master Du said: 'According to the edict, after pacification you are to join in a covenant; Imjon, though not yet surrendered, can be sworn with.' Silla thought: according to the edict, it is 'after pacification' that they are to join in covenant; Imjon had not yet surrendered, so it could not be considered 'pacified.' Moreover Baekje was treacherous in a hundred ways, changeable and inconsistent; even if we made a covenant with them now, I feared the trouble of 'biting one's navel' later, and so I asked by memorial that the covenant be halted. In the first year of Lingde, a strict edict was handed down again, blaming us for not swearing the covenant, and so we sent men to Ungnyeong to build an altar and join in the covenant. At the place of the covenant the two borders were made. Though the covenant was not what we wished, we dared not disobey the edict. Again at Mt. Chwiri an altar was built, and before the imperial envoy Liu Renyuan we smeared blood and swore, taking the mountains and rivers as our oath, drew the boundary and set up markers, to be boundaries forever, with the people living there and each pursuing his own livelihood. In the second year of Qianfeng, hearing that Grand Commander the Duke of Ying was campaigning against Liaodong, I went to Hanseong Province and sent troops to assemble at the border. Silla's troops could not enter alone, so we first sent scouts three times, dispatched by boats in succession, to watch for the great army. The scouts came back and all said, 'The great army has not reached Pyongyang.' Meanwhile we attacked Goguryeo's Chiljung Fortress and opened the road, waiting for the great army to arrive. The fortress was just about to fall when Duke Ying's messenger Gang Sim came and said: 'On the orders of the Grand Commander, Silla's troops need not attack fortresses; go quickly to Pyongyang, and grain will be provided.' I sent troops to the rendezvous, and when they reached Sugok Fortress they heard that the great army had already withdrawn, and Silla's troops at once pulled back. In the third year of Qianfeng, I sent the Daegam Kim Bo-ga by sea to obtain Duke Ying's orders. On receiving the orders, Silla's troops were to assemble at Pyongyang. In the fifth month Right Minister Liu came, and Silla's troops were dispatched to go with him to Pyongyang. I too went to Hanseong Province to inspect the troops. At this time the barbarian and Han armies all gathered at the Sa River, and Namgeon sent out troops, wishing to settle matters in one battle. Silla's troops alone formed the vanguard and first broke the great formation, and within Pyongyang city the edge was blunted and spirit drawn in. Afterward Duke Ying took another five hundred of Silla's brave cavalry to enter the city gate first, and so Pyongyang was broken and the great achievement completed. Upon this Silla's soldiers all said: 'Since the campaigns began nine years have passed and human strength is exhausted; finally pacifying both countries, a long hope of generations, is fulfilled today. Surely our country will receive the grace of loyal service and our men the reward of effort.' But Duke Ying let slip: 'Silla earlier missed the military date; that too must be reckoned.' When Silla's soldiers heard these words, their fear grew still greater. Furthermore the commanders who had earned merit were all recorded and brought to court; when they arrived at the capital, it was said, 'Now Silla has no merit at all.' When the commanders returned, the people grew still more afraid. Also Piryeol Fortress was originally Silla's; Goguryeo had seized it thirty years or more before, and Silla recovered the fortress, moved people there, set up officials to guard it, and yet this fortress was taken again and given back to Goguryeo. Silla has, since pacifying Baekje until settling Goguryeo, given loyal service and effort and never failed the state; we do not know what crime it was that we were cast aside in one morning. Though suffering such injustice, we have never had a rebellious heart. In the first year of Zongzhang, Baekje at the covenant site moved the boundary markers and changed the signs, encroaching on our fields; it enticed our slaves and lured our people, hiding them in the interior, and though we repeatedly demanded their return, in the end they were not returned. They also sent word: 'The state is repairing ships, ostensibly to attack the Wa country, but in fact wishes to attack Silla.' The people, hearing this, were alarmed and uneasy. They also married a Baekje woman to Silla's governor of Hanseong, Bak Do-yu, plotted together, and stole Silla's weapons to make a surprise attack on a province; thanks to the plot being discovered, Do-yu was at once beheaded and the scheme failed. In the sixth month of the first year of Xianheng, Goguryeo plotted rebellion and killed all the Han officials. Silla wished to send troops and first informed Ungjin: 'Goguryeo has already rebelled and must be attacked; we are both subjects of the emperor, and it is right that we jointly punish the vicious rebels. As to sending troops, there must be consultation; please send officials here to plan together.' The Baekje Sima Ye Gun came here, and together they agreed: 'After troops are sent, we fear mutual suspicion; the officials of both places should exchange hostages.' We at once sent Kim Yu-don, together with the Baekje registrars Sumi and Jang-gwi of the prefectural city, to the prefecture to discuss the matter of exchanging hostages. Though Baekje agreed to exchange hostages, it nevertheless gathered troops in the city, and came below that city and attacked by night. In the seventh month the envoy to court Kim Heum-sun and others arrived, and as the boundary lands were about to be drawn, they examined the maps and inspected the old lands of Baekje, and ordered that all be ceded back. The Yellow River had not yet become a belt nor Mt. Tai a whetstone, yet within three or four years a thing was given and then taken away; the people of Silla all lost their hope, and said: 'Silla and Baekje have been deep enemies for generations; seeing the state of Baekje now, it will surely set up a separate state, and after a hundred years our descendants will be swallowed and destroyed. Silla is already a province of the empire and should not be divided into two countries. We wish to be one family, with no trouble afterward forever.' Last year in the ninth month, I recorded the circumstances in full and sent envoys to report, but they were blown off course and returned. I sent envoys again, but they could not arrive either. Later, with cold wind and rapid waves, there was no time to report. Baekje fabricated a memorial: 'Silla has rebelled.' Silla, having earlier lost the favour of the honoured ministers and later suffered Baekje's slander, is blamed whether advancing or retreating, and has not been able to state its loyal sincerity. Plausible slander passes daily to the sage's hearing, while loyalty without two minds has never once reached it. Your envoy Rimyun has come with your honoured letter, and I understand that the Commander braved wind and waves and came far overseas; properly I should have sent envoys to welcome you at the suburb and presented ox and wine, but dwelling far away in a different city I have not been able to show the courtesy, and I have at times missed the welcome; I beg that you not take it amiss. Reading the Commander's letter, which treats Silla wholly as already rebellious, I was startled and afraid, for this is not my true heart. Counting my own efforts, I feared the ridicule of receiving such disgrace; to close my mouth and accept the rebuke would also fall among those who are unpitied; so now I briefly set forth the injustice, recording in full that we have not rebelled. The state did not send down a single envoy to ask the origin, but at once sent tens of thousands of troops to overturn our lair; tower ships fill the blue sea, prows and sterns link at the river mouth, reckoning Ungjin and attacking Silla. Alas! When the two countries were not yet settled, we were driven like hounds that point the trail; now that the wild beasts are exhausted, we instead see the pressure of being boiled and slaughtered. Baekje, which ravaged us, has instead received the reward of Yongchi, while Silla, which gave itself to Han, has already seen the execution of Ding Gong. Though the light of the great sun does not turn back, the heart of the sunflower still faces the sun. The Commander is endowed with the heroic qi and the talent of a general and minister; the seven virtues together, the nine schools read; respectfully carrying out Heaven's punishment, he has wrongly imposed an offence that is not. Before the heavenly troops set out, first ask for the origin; on the occasion of this letter I dare to state that we have not rebelled, and I beg the Commander to consider carefully and report in full by memorial. Respectfully stated by Kim Beop-min, King of Silla, Grand Governor of Rimju, General of the Left Guard, Equal to the Three Offices, Supreme Pillar of the State."
